explain: Evidence that is not in the alert is invented, whatever the model's confidence. Editing the alert to fit the model corrupts the record, and closing on a rejected reply is the outcome the check exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: When not to automate, and a design review checklist
question: Which step fits 'robot prepares, human approves'?
options: Adding asset and identity context to every new alert
Opening a case for each new alert
Sending the company-wide breach notification email
Isolating one employee laptop from the network after a confirmed malicious download
explain: Isolation disrupts one person and is awkward to undo, so a quick human check is worth it, but the blast radius is one machine and speed matters. Enrichment and case creation are safe to automate fully; a company-wide breach notice is a human decision from start to finish.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
question: A company's main worry is ransomware affiliates. Which control best reduces that specific threat?
options: A bigger firewall rule set for outbound web traffic only
Hiding the company's logo from its website
Encrypting the data at rest on servers
Offline backups plus removing unused remote-access accounts
explain: Affiliates commonly enter through exposed remote access with stolen credentials and profit by making data unavailable. Removing unused access shrinks their entry points, and offline backups (which CISA's DarkSide advisory recommends) remove the leverage. Encryption at rest does not stop ransomware from encrypting the data again.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Equifax 2017: a known bug and a missed patch
question: Struts 2.5.10 is installed. Is it vulnerable to CVE-2017-5638?
options: No: 2.5.10 is newer than 2.3.32
No: only 2.3.x was affected
It depends on the CVSS score
Yes: on the 2.5 branch the first fixed version is 2.5.10.1
explain: NVD lists 2.5.x before 2.5.10.1 as affected. Comparing across branches (2.5.10 against 2.3.32) is the classic mistake; compare within the branch.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
question: Under the Supreme Court's reading in Van Buren, which act most clearly 'exceeds authorized access'?
options: An employee reads a report they are allowed to read, for a personal reason
A user forgets to log out
A researcher reads a public security.txt file
A logged-in user changes an ID in a URL to open another customer's records that are off-limits to them
explain: The Court tied 'exceeds authorized access' to entering areas of a computer, such as files or databases, that are off-limits to you. Reading another customer's records fits; misusing data you may see is the case the Court excluded.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: From gaps to a roadmap: strategy, sequencing and dependencies
question: Which statement is a strategy rather than a wish?
options: We will be world-class in security
We will improve our posture across all areas this year
For 12 months identity and recovery come first; we will not start a DLP programme this year
Security is everyone's responsibility
explain: Only that option contains a diagnosis-driven choice and an explicit thing not to do, which lets people decide what to stop asking for. The others cannot guide a single resource decision.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Designing the team: functions, coverage and where people sit
question: Why does one 24x7 seat need about 5 people rather than 168 / 40 = 4.2?
options: Because night shifts are shorter by law
Because MDR vendors require it
Because each analyst actually works fewer than 52 x 40 hours once leave, holidays, sickness and training are removed
Because the script rounds up twice
explain: 168 / 40 assumes every person works every week of the year. With 48 days away (in the example), one person works 1,696 hours, so 8,760 / 1,696 = 5.17, rounded up to 6 people.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Regulators and disclosure: materiality, risk factors, certifications
question: Under NYDFS Part 500 as amended in 2023, who signs the annual certification of compliance?
options: Any senior officer
The external auditor
The board chair alone
The highest-ranking executive and the CISO
explain: Section 500.17(b)(2) requires the highest-ranking executive and the CISO (or, without a CISO, the senior officer responsible for the programme). It must rest on documentation kept for five years.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Writing a finding: title, impact, evidence, fix
question: Which finding title is most useful in a ticket list read by an engineering manager?
options: Critical vulnerability found during testing
Burp Suite scanner result #44
CVE-style issue in API
Missing ownership check on /api/invoices/{id} exposes all customers' invoices
explain: It names the weakness, the location and the consequence, so the manager can route it and judge urgency without opening it. The others say nothing about what or where.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Risk memos and exceptions: making someone own the decision
question: Who should sign a risk acceptance for an unpatched customer-facing system?
options: The security engineer who found it
Whoever is on call that week
Nobody; acceptances should be verbal
The designated risk owner, who is accountable for the business outcome and has authority to accept it
explain: NIST IR 8286 defines the risk owner as the party responsible and accountable. Security advises and records; the owner decides. A security engineer accepting business risk is deciding something they do not own.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Getting a fix shipped when you cannot order it
question: A team ignores a High finding for six weeks. What is the most effective next message?
options: A broadcast email to the whole engineering department
Silently lower the severity so the backlog looks better
Fix it yourself in production without telling them
A message to the team lead offering the ready fix or an exception, with a date, and naming the pre-agreed escalation if neither happens
explain: It makes the cheapest path obvious, gives the owner a real choice including a formal exception, and uses a known escalation route rather than public shaming or unilateral action.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inside the search tree: selection, expansion, evaluation and backup
question: In a two-player search, the backup adds +v to every edge on the path, where v is the value for the player to move at the leaf. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; Q is symmetric between players
The search spends too many visits on the prior
Every second level is credited from the wrong player's view, so selection there favors moves that help the opponent
Visit counts stop growing
explain: The player to move at the leaf did not choose the last edge; the opponent did. Crediting that edge with +v rewards the opponent's move for being good for you. Flipping the sign at each ply keeps every Q in the chooser's point of view.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
question: In SPIN's idealized update, set lambda = 1. What happens after one iteration?
options: The model moves halfway toward the data distribution
The model becomes exactly p_data, and further iterations change nothing
The model overshoots p_data and oscillates
Nothing, because lambda = 1 cancels the loss
explain: With 1/lambda = 1 the update is p_t times p_data / p_t, which is p_data after renormalizing. Then the ratio is 1 everywhere and the update is the identity. Real training cannot represent the ideal update exactly, which is one reason SPIN needs several iterations.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof
question: AlphaProof's training problems come from an auto-formalizer that sometimes mistranslates the original problem. Why does this not corrupt the training signal?
options: Mistranslated statements are removed by a human reviewer
Any Lean statement is a real problem: Lean checks whatever proof or disproof is found, so each attempt is labeled correctly even if it is not the intended problem
The value head learns to ignore mistranslated problems
Test-time RL replaces the main RL data
explain: The paper notes that each auto-formalized statement, faithful or not, is a valid formal problem to prove or disprove. The judge, Lean's kernel, is exact about the statement actually given, so the experience is always correctly labeled.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
question: In the token-level example, keeping the top half of tokens dropped "pm" from "3 pm". Which change best fixes this?
options: Use a larger percentile so fewer tokens are kept
Score and filter phrase-level units, so "3 pm" is kept or dropped as a whole
Use a bigger target LLM
Drop the most surprising tokens instead
explain: "pm" is predictable once you have seen "3", so it has little self-information on its own, yet the unit "3 pm" carries the meaning. Selective Context merges tokens into phrases or sentences for this reason, and LLMLingua's budget controller likewise works at coarser levels first.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: IMDSv2: session tokens, PUT and a hop limit of 1
question: Why does IMDSv2 refuse to issue a token to a PUT that carries an X-Forwarded-For header?
options: The header is how open reverse proxies normally mark relayed requests, so its presence means the request probably came from outside
The header makes the token too long
AWS SDKs never send any headers
It prevents IPv6 requests
explain: Reverse proxies add X-Forwarded-For to tell the back end who the original caller was. Legitimate local software has no reason to send it, so its presence is a cheap and reliable signal that the request was relayed.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Insecure deserialization: when loading data runs code
question: Which design removes the deserialization risk entirely for a session cookie that stores a user's theme and language?
options: Store JSON with two fields, validate both against allowed values, and sign it with an HMAC
Pickle the settings and Base64-encode them
Pickle the settings but rename the cookie
Use Java serialization with a longer key
explain: JSON parsing creates only data, the allowlist check bounds the values, and the HMAC stops tampering. Base64 or renaming changes nothing about what pickle.loads will execute.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: File uploads: names, types, storage and execution
question: An upload endpoint checks that the Content-Type header is image/jpeg and the file name ends in .jpg, then saves to the web root under the original name. Which is the most serious remaining problem?
options: Both checks trust attacker-controlled values, and the name and location still let a crafted file be served or executed from the web root
JPEG files can be large
The check should accept image/jpg too
JPEG has no magic bytes
explain: The header is written by the client, and the name is chosen by the client. Check the content, generate the name, and store outside the web root so even a file that slips through can never run.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: HiCache: a radix tree that spans GPU, host memory and storage
question: Two SGLang instances run on different nodes, each with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 4` and no storage backend. A chat's next turn is routed to the other instance than before. Why does it miss the cache?
options: The router hashes prompts, so the two instances never see the same prefix
Host memory (L2) is private to each instance; only an L3 backend that both instances share could carry the history across
A ratio of 4 is too small to hold a chat history
HiCache only keeps KV in host memory under the write_back policy
explain: L1 and L2 belong to one instance's process. The first instance may still hold the history in host memory, but the second cannot read it. Attaching a shared backend such as Mooncake or 3FS (with the same namespace on both) makes L3 hits possible; routing the turn back to the first instance also works.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Why can't the scheduler simply build batch k+1 while batch k runs, with no extra machinery?
options: Batch k+1 needs batch k's sampled tokens as its inputs, which are not known until batch k finishes; SGLang uses future-token placeholders resolved on the GPU
The GPU cannot run two kernels in a row
Python cannot start a second thread
The radix tree must be rebuilt from scratch every step
explain: For decoding, each step's input is the previous step's output. Overlap therefore needs a way to refer to tokens that do not exist yet. The release notes describe resolving this dependency with future tokens and careful CUDA event synchronization.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Dijkstra's algorithm: settle nodes in order of distance
question: Suppose one arc had weight -5 (say, a modeled time bonus). What breaks?
options: Correctness: a settled node's label might later be beaten through the negative arc
Only performance: the answer stays correct but slower
Nothing, as long as there is no negative cycle
The priority queue cannot store negative keys
explain: The finality argument assumes the rest of any path adds nonnegative length. A negative arc can make a path through a far node cheaper than an already settled label. Label-correcting methods, which may lower a label many times, handle negative weights at higher cost: Bellman-Ford makes up to one round fewer than there are vertices, relaxing every arc in each round, so its time grows with vertices times arcs.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Sampling: why a 7 Hz wave sampled at 10 Hz looks like 3 Hz
question: You have 1000 Hz sensor data and want 100 Hz. A colleague writes `y = x[::10]`, Python slicing that keeps every 10th sample. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: keeping every 10th sample is exactly what downsampling means
Content between 50 and 500 Hz folds into the 0 to 50 Hz band, because nothing removed it first
The result has the wrong length; it should be `x[::100]`
Slicing shifts the phase by half a sample, which is the only error
explain: Keeping every 10th sample makes the new Nyquist frequency 50 Hz. Anything in the original data between 50 and 500 Hz now aliases into 0 to 50 Hz. Low-pass filter first, or use `scipy.signal.decimate(x, 10)`, which filters then downsamples.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
question: How many 8-bit integers does one AVX-512 `zmm` register hold, and how many 64-bit doubles?
options: 64 and 8
16 and 2
32 and 4
explain: 512 bits / 8 bits = 64 bytes, and 512 / 64 = 8 doubles. 512 and 64 would be counting bits, not lanes; 16 and 2 is the 128-bit case.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
question: The same SVE saxpy binary runs with n = 10 on a 128-bit and a 512-bit implementation. How many loop iterations does each run?
options: 3 and 1
10 and 10
3 and 3, because the binary was compiled for 128 bits
2 and 1
explain: With 4 lanes the loop runs at i = 0, 4, 8 (the last with T T F F). With 16 lanes one iteration covers all 10 elements under a 10-true predicate. The lane count is read at run time by incw and svcntw.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
question: A bump pointer sits at offset 13 in a chunk. The next request is 16 bytes with alignment 8. At which offset does the object start, and where does the pointer end up (bumping upwards)?
options: Starts at 13, pointer ends at 29
Starts at 16, pointer ends at 32
Starts at 8, pointer ends at 24
Starts at 16, pointer ends at 29
explain: Round 13 up to a multiple of 8: 13 + 7 = 20, and clearing the low 3 bits (20 AND NOT 7) gives 16. Then add the size: 16 + 16 = 32. The 3 bytes at offsets 13 to 15 are padding.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
question: You have a fixed 64-GPU budget for a math RLVR run with a synchronous loop and short, similar-length responses. Which placement fits the GLM-4.5 report's guidance?
options: 32 rollout GPUs and 32 training GPUs in separate pools, synchronous
Colocated with --colocate, so all 64 GPUs alternate between rollout and training
Separate pools with fully async rollout and maximal staleness
Rollout-only, with training on CPU
explain: For reasoning tasks the report uses colocated synchronous training with dynamic sampling. A synchronous loop on split pools leaves each half idle while the other works.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
question: Rollout takes 300 s, training 300 s and sync 48 s per round on separate pools. Ignoring all overheads, what is the best case for fully async?
options: 348 s per round, about 1.86x faster than 648 s
648 s per round, the same as sync
300 s per round
48 s per round
explain: The bound is max(t_R, t_T) + t_W = 300 + 48 = 348 s against 300 + 300 + 48 = 648 s serial. Weight sync is not hidden in this model, so the round cannot drop to 300 s.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: What a blockchain is: a shared ledger that nobody owns
question: Which of these does a working blockchain guarantee by itself?
options: That a contract's code has no bugs
That a price fed into a contract is true
That an agreed history of transactions is very costly to rewrite
That the private key signing a transaction is held by its rightful owner
explain: Hash linking plus consensus protects recorded history. Code bugs, false inputs (the oracle problem) and stolen keys are outside that guarantee, and they cause most losses.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: A toy chain in Python, and thinking in invariants
question: Which is a useful invariant for a token contract?
options: The contract has been audited
The sum of all balances equals totalSupply
Gas used per transfer is under 50,000
The owner is an EOA
explain: An invariant is a property of the state that every transaction must preserve. Gas use and audits are not properties of the state, and the owner's account type says nothing about correctness.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Price oracles, spot prices and flash loans
question: Why is a TWAP built from start-of-block prices harder to manipulate with a flash loan?
options: Flash loans are banned during TWAP windows
The loan must be repaid within one transaction, but the price is only sampled before any trades in a block
TWAPs use Chainlink internally
TWAPs ignore large trades
explain: A flash-loan trade is reversed inside one transaction, so it never sits at the start of a block. Moving a TWAP means holding a bad price across blocks, at real cost and risk.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Keys, multisigs and blind signing: Bybit 2025
question: Three Bybit signers each used their own device and key. Why did requiring three signatures not stop the theft?
options: The attacker had stolen all three private keys
Safe ignores the signature threshold for delegatecall
All three relied on the same compromised web app to show and prepare the transaction, and signed data they could not read
The cold wallet only needed one signature
explain: The keys were never stolen. The shared front end was, and blind signing meant no signer could see that the transaction was a delegatecall to an unknown contract.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
question: A rule fires because a user typed the wrong password three times. Using the NIST definitions, what is it so far?
options: An event that may be an adverse event; triage decides whether anything jeopardised systems or data
An incident, because a security rule fired
A false positive, because wrong passwords are normal
Nothing worth recording
explain: Failed logins are events. Whether they are adverse, and whether they add up to an incident (a password-guessing attack that succeeded, say), is exactly what triage decides. Calling it an incident or a false positive before looking skips the work.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
question: Impossible travel fires: a sign-in from Paris, then from Toronto 40 minutes later. Both passed MFA by the same phone, the Toronto IP belongs to the company's VPN provider, and the user agent and device ID match the user's laptop. Best verdict?
options: True positive: credentials stolen
False positive: the haversine formula is wrong
Undetermined: escalate to incident response
Benign true positive: the travel is impossible for a person but explained by the VPN; record it and suggest adding the VPN egress to the rule's known locations
explain: The rule correctly measured an impossible speed between two IPs, so it is not a false positive. The context (company VPN, same device, MFA passed on the user's phone) explains it, so it is benign. The note should feed a context fix, not a rule deletion.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
question: Mandiant's Snowflake investigation found that most stolen credentials had been exposed by infostealers long before use, some since 2020. Which control would have made those old credentials useless regardless of when they leaked?
options: Longer log retention
Requiring MFA (and network allow lists) on the accounts
A larger SOC team
Geolocation-based alerting
explain: Mandiant names missing MFA, unrotated credentials and missing network allow lists as the three factors. MFA and allow lists block a leaked password outright; logging and staffing only help you notice afterwards.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
question: Which first line suits an update to leadership at hour two of an incident?
options: "We have run 140 queries across 6 data sources."
"Attack by a sophisticated nation-state."
"One laptop and one account compromised; contained; no evidence yet of data loss; next update 14:00 UTC."
"Too early to say anything."
explain: Bottom line first: impact, containment status, what is still unknown, when they will hear next. Activity counts tell leaders nothing, unsupported attribution misleads, and silence breeds rumours.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Why Johnny can't encrypt: usability is a security property
question: Which of Whitten and Tygar's properties explains why one accidental plaintext email is so serious?
options: The abstraction property
The barn door property
The unmotivated user property
The lack of feedback property
explain: Once the secret has been sent unprotected, nobody can be sure it was not read. Prevention has to happen before the mistake, because no fix after it restores secrecy.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing
question: A manager receives a voice message that sounds exactly like the CEO asking for an urgent transfer, followed by a text from a new number. Which response matches the IC3's guidance?
options: Reply to the text asking a personal question only the CEO would know
Listen for audio glitches; if none, proceed
Forward the voice message to a deepfake detection website and proceed if it says genuine
Call the CEO on a number already on record and confirm before doing anything
explain: The IC3 advises independently finding the person's number and calling to verify, and verifying new contact details through a previously confirmed channel. Personal questions can be researched, and detection is unreliable.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules
question: A building has three nested areas, and every door, including the server room, accepts a badge tap alone. Against NIST SP 800-116's table, what is wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as the badges are encrypted
The limited and exclusion areas get only one factor instead of the two and three they need
There are too many doors
Badges should only be used at the front door
explain: Repeating the same factor at every door proves nothing new. The limited area needs two factors and the exclusion area three, for example badge plus PIN plus fingerprint.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
question: Before a physical test of a regional office, which ROE check would most directly have prevented the Iowa arrests?
options: Confirm that the client controls the building and that any other authority with jurisdiction has agreed or been informed
Use quieter tools
Test only during business hours
Wear company uniforms
explain: The conflict was over who controlled the courthouse and who had been told. Hours and attire matter, but authorisation from every party with control is the foundation.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: Why does Scaling Monosemanticity multiply each latent's activation by its decoder norm inside the sparsity penalty?
options: To make the encoder run faster
So the SAE cannot lower the penalty by shrinking activations while growing decoder columns, which would leave reconstructions unchanged
To force exactly k latents to be active
Because decoder norms equal the language model's loss
explain: Scaling f_i down by c and d_i up by c leaves f_i d_i (and so x-hat) unchanged but cuts a plain L1 penalty by c. Weighting by the decoder norm makes the penalty invariant to that rescaling. A unit-norm constraint on decoder columns achieves the same thing.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
question: Which check would most directly test the name 'promotes the token Paris' for a residual-stream latent?
options: Count how often the latent fires
Clamp the latent higher on prompts where it is off and measure whether the probability of ' Paris' rises
Raise its autointerp detection score
Look at its top five activating examples again
explain: The name is a claim about what the latent writes. An intervention measures that causally; activation-based scores and density only describe where it fires. The logit effect suggests it, and the clamp confirms it through the real network.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
question: A colleague says nearest neighbor is safest because it never invents values that were not measured. What is the main weakness of the resulting map?
options: It cannot be computed without a fitted variogram
It is discontinuous: the value jumps at Voronoi cell borders even when the true field is smooth
It always returns the global mean far from sensors
It gives every sensor the same weight
explain: Nearest neighbor copies the closest reading, so the map is a set of flat Voronoi tiles with steps at the borders. It needs no model, and far from sensors it still copies the nearest one rather than the mean.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
question: You have 5,000 weather stations and need a 1 km map nightly. Global ordinary kriging is too slow. Which change keeps most of kriging's benefits?
options: Switch to nearest neighbor
Krige from a local neighborhood of the nearest few dozen stations per target, using a variogram fitted once on all stations
Drop the variogram and set all weights to 1/5000
Use IDW with p = 0
explain: Local neighborhoods (like scikit-gstat's max_points or RBFInterpolator's neighbors) make each solve small. Distant stations get negligible weight beyond the range anyway, so the map changes little while cost drops sharply.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
question: Which change raises the maximum achievable speedup when the draft is free (c = 0)?
options: Increasing gamma beyond 20
Lowering the target's temperature has no effect
Using a bigger GPU for the draft
Raising alpha, because the speedup is capped by 1/(1 - alpha)
explain: With c = 0 the speedup is the expected tokens per pass, bounded by 1/(1 - alpha) however large gamma gets. Only better acceptance raises the cap; lower temperature usually helps because it sharpens both distributions.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts and prompt lookup decoding
question: An EAGLE-1-style drafter has a high acceptance rate at draft position 1 but much lower at positions 3 and 4. Which explanation fits best?
options: The target's LM head is less accurate deep into a draft
Exposure bias: from step 2 on, the drafter's inputs include its own predicted features, which it never saw in training, and errors compound
Tree attention masks hide earlier draft tokens
Position 1 is always accepted because it is the bonus token
explain: Each later step feeds the drafter its own estimates instead of target features. EAGLE-3's training-time test simulates those steps during training, and the paper reports its acceptance rate stays almost flat as more inputs come from the drafter.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: Whisper's timestamp tokens are quantized to the native resolution. A word starts at 1.234 s. What is the closest timestamp the model can emit?
explain: Each encoder position covers 20 ms (30 s / 1500), and timestamp tokens are on the same 20 ms grid: ..., 1.22, 1.24, ... The nearest grid point to 1.234 s is 1.24 s. Finer word timings need extra machinery, such as the cross-attention alignment the openai/whisper code offers for word timestamps.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
question: A function returns `&x`, where `x` is one of its local variables. The caller reads the pointer immediately and gets the right value, but after calling `printf` it reads garbage. Why?
options: The compiler moved x to the heap, and printf freed it
x's frame was released on return; printf's own frame reused those stack bytes
Reading a stack variable from another function always raises SIGSEGV
The red zone is cleared by the kernel on every return
explain: Returning only moves `rsp` back up; the bytes are not erased, so an immediate read may look fine. The next call (here `printf`) pushes its frame into the same addresses and overwrites them. No fault occurs because the memory is still mapped, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. The red zone is never cleared by the kernel.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
question: A machine has 16 GiB of RAM, no swap and `vm.overcommit_memory = 0`. Processes A and B each malloc 12 GiB and each writes only its first 1 GiB. What most likely happens?
options: B's malloc returns NULL because 24 GiB exceeds RAM
Both mallocs succeed and both run normally: only touched pages use RAM
Both succeed, then the OOM killer immediately kills one of them
The kernel zeroes 24 GiB at malloc time and the machine swaps
explain: The default heuristic only rejects a single request bigger than RAM plus swap; 12 GiB is not, and it does not add up other processes' reservations. Frames are allocated on first touch, so about 2 GiB of RAM is used. Only if A and B actually wrote more than RAM holds would the OOM killer step in.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Where to add it, at which tokens, and how hard
question: A vector extracted at layer 6 of a 48-layer model works well at c = 4. A colleague adds the same vector at layer 40 with c = 4 and sees almost no effect. What is the most likely explanation?
options: At layer 40 the residual stream is much larger, so the same c is a much smaller relative push, and the concept may be represented differently there
Steering vectors only work in the first half of a network
Adding at a later layer reverses the sign of the vector
The model detects the vector and removes it
explain: Residual norms grow with depth, so a fixed-size vector becomes relatively small; on top of that, a direction found at layer 6 need not be the direction the concept uses at layer 40. Extract and inject at the same layer, and sweep c relative to the local norm.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: When steering fails: unreliable inputs and the prompting baseline
question: A team's refusal vector lowers the average refusal rate on held-out prompts from 60% to 20%. Which extra measurement best tests whether it is reliable?
options: The per-prompt slope of the behavior against the coefficient, and the fraction of prompts with a negative slope
A larger coefficient, to see whether the rate reaches 0%
The same average measured on the prompts used to build the vector
The norm of the vector compared with the residual stream
explain: Tan et al. show averages can hide many inputs that move the wrong way. Per-input slopes reveal that distribution directly. A larger coefficient changes the effect size, not its reliability; building-set scores leak; the norm ratio sets a scale but says nothing about consistency.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
question: Rerun the toy with B = 7 s instead of 2 s (L still 5 s). Which readings are late or dropped?
options: e6 and e10 late, e12 dropped, exactly as before
No reading is late, and e12 is still dropped
Nothing is late or dropped
Every out-of-order reading is dropped
explain: When e6 arrives, max = 13 so W = 6 < 10: on time. When e10 arrives, max = 22 so W = 15 < 20: on time. e12 arrives with W = 27 - 7 = 20, past 10 + 5 = 15: still dropped. The price: window [0,10) now first fires at processing time 22.5 s (when e9 arrives) instead of 13.4 s.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Why did the Transformer use scaled dot-product scores instead of Bahdanau's additive scores?
options: Both cost about the same in theory, but the dot product runs as one fast matrix multiplication; scaling fixes its weakness at large d_k
Additive scores cannot be trained with gradient descent
Dot products need no learned parameters at all, so the model is smaller
Additive scores only work with RNN hidden states
explain: Section 3.2.1 says the two have similar theoretical complexity and that dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice. Without scaling, additive attention wins for large d_k, so the paper divides by the square root of d_k. The queries and keys are still produced by learned projections.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Relative positions: from sinusoids to RoPE and ALiBi
question: A model uses RoPE. A query at position 100 and a key at position 97 have score 2.3. The same query and key vectors are placed at positions 1003 and 1000. What is the score?
options: Lower, because RoPE scores decay with absolute position
2.3, because only the offset (3) enters the score
Unpredictable, because angles like 1003 theta wrap around many times
Higher, because later positions get larger rotations
explain: The rotations by 1003 theta and 1000 theta cancel down to a rotation by the offset, exactly as for 100 and 97, so the score is identical. Wrapping is harmless here because only the difference of angles enters. Long-term decay is about the distance between the two tokens, not about where they sit.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
question: Why does the long document C score high under TF-IDF even though it is not more focused on the query?
options: Its IDF values are higher
TF-IDF divides by document length, which favors long documents
C contains both query terms, and TF-IDF only scores documents with all terms
Longer documents have more tokens, so their raw counts are larger for many terms
explain: IDF depends only on the term, not the document. TF-IDF as written does not divide by length at all, and it scores any document with at least one term (A, B and D are scored too). C wins because a 60-token document simply has room for more occurrences.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
question: A teammate's first logged loss on the 65-character model is 27. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is already overfitting
The data loader is shifting targets by two
The initialization makes some logits huge, so the model is confidently wrong
Nothing: 27 is typical for an untrained character model
explain: An untrained model with small weights should print about ln 65 = 4.17. A much larger loss means a very low probability on the true token, which only happens when logits are large and spread out, typically from weights initialized with too large a scale.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: You start GPT-2 small at the peak rate 6e-4 with no warmup and the loss spikes to NaN within 100 steps. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Increase weight decay to 1.0
Add a linear warmup over the first few thousand steps
Remove gradient clipping
Switch from cosine decay to a constant rate
explain: In the first steps Adam's running statistics are still settling, so full-size updates can blow up a freshly initialized model. Warmup ramps the step size meanwhile, which is why nanoGPT warms up for 2,000 steps. Xiong et al. find pre-LN models like GPT-2 less fragile here than post-LN ones, but warmup remains the standard fix. Removing clipping or raising decay does not touch the cause, and the decay shape only matters later.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
question: A sampling script uses `logits[logits <= v[:, [-1]]] = -inf` (note `<=`) with top_k = 5. What happens?
options: Nothing changes; < and <= behave the same
The 5th-largest logit (and any ties with it) is also removed, so only 4 tokens survive; with top_k = 1 every logit is masked and softmax returns NaN
Top-k now keeps 6 tokens
Temperature stops having an effect
explain: v[:, [-1]] is the k-th largest logit, the threshold that must survive. With <= it is thrown away too, leaving k - 1 choices, and for k = 1 nothing survives: all minus infinity gives NaN probabilities and multinomial fails.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: The multivariable chain rule: summing over every path
question: $f = x y + x$ with $x = 2$, $y = 5$. What is $\partial f / \partial x$?
options: 5, from the product term only
6: the path through the product gives y = 5 and the added x gives 1
1, from the added x only
7, which is x + y
explain: $x$ reaches $f$ by two paths. Through $xy$ the local rate is $y = 5$; through the bare $+ x$ term it is 1. The paths add: $5 + 1 = 6$. Keeping only one path is the fan-out mistake.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
question: A model has 1 million parameters. Roughly how many forward evaluations of the loss does a centered finite-difference gradient need, compared with backprop?
options: About 2, the same as backprop
About 2 million, versus one forward plus one backward pass for backprop
About 1000, the square root of the parameter count
Exactly 1 million, versus 1 million backward passes for backprop
explain: Centered differences need two evaluations per parameter, $2 \times 10^6$ forward passes. Reverse-mode differentiation gets the whole gradient of a scalar loss from one forward and one backward pass, which is why finite differences are only used to spot-check gradients.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
question: After `f() { echo 5; return 3; }` and `y=$(f)`, what are y and `$?`?
options: y is 5 and `$?` is 3
y is 3 and `$?` is 0
y is 5 and `$?` is 0
y is 53 and `$?` is 0
explain: Command substitution captures what f prints, 5. The return value is not output; it becomes the exit status, and an assignment whose value came from `$(...)` takes that command's status, 3 (a real bash run printed `y=5 status=3`).

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
question: A CI step runs `pytest | tee test.log` (tee copies its input to the screen and to a file) and always shows green even when tests fail. What is the minimal fix?
options: Replace `|` with `&&`
Add `set -u`
Add `set -o pipefail` before the command
Redirect with `2>&1` instead of piping
explain: The pipeline's status is tee's, which succeeds. pipefail makes the pipeline report the rightmost non-zero status, so pytest's failure surfaces. `&&` would stop tee from seeing the output stream at all.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: A balanced binary tree holds a vocabulary of $W = 1{,}048{,}576 = 2^{20}$ words at its leaves. How many sigmoid decisions does hierarchical softmax make to score one word?
explain: The path from the root to a leaf in a balanced tree of $2^{20}$ leaves has 20 inner nodes, one sigmoid each, instead of a million dot products. A Huffman tree is not balanced: frequent words get shorter paths and rare words longer ones, which lowers the average cost on real text.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying
question: Your product catalog adds thousands of new item IDs every day, and the model uses one learned embedding row per ID. What problem should you expect for brand-new items?
options: Their rows are still at their random initialization because they have received no gradient, so their similarities are meaningless
None, embeddings generalize to any ID
They will all collapse to the zero vector
Their vectors will equal the average of all rows
explain: A row learns only when its ID appears in training. New IDs keep their random initial vectors (in PyTorch drawn from N(0, 1)). Systems handle this cold-start problem with a shared unknown or hashed row, or by building vectors from content features, the same idea fastText uses with character n-grams in the next lesson.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Contrastive training in practice: in-batch negatives and collapse
question: Which of these objectives is minimized by an encoder that maps every image to the same vector?
options: Alignment alone, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}$
NT-Xent with in-batch negatives
Uniformity, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{uniform}}$
MoCo's loss with a queue of negatives
explain: A constant encoder puts every positive pair at distance 0, the minimum of alignment. Every loss that includes negatives or a uniformity term penalizes it: NT-Xent costs ln(2N - 1) per row, and uniformity reaches its maximum, 0.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Fewer bytes per weight: number formats and weight-only quantization
question: LLaMA-7B moves from FP16 to INT4 weight-only quantization on an A100. Roughly what happens to the time to first token for a 4,000-token prompt?
options: It drops about 4x, like the decode floor
Almost nothing: prefill needs about 53.6 TFLOP, about 172 ms of math, and weight reads (6.6 ms in FP16) were already hidden under it
It doubles, because dequantizing costs extra FLOPs
It drops 2x, because INT4 math is twice as fast
explain: Prefill of 4,000 tokens is $2\times6.7\times10^9\times4000\approx53.6$ TFLOP, about 172 ms at 312 TFLOP/s. Reading the weights took only 6.6 ms in FP16 and is overlapped with that math. Weight-only INT4 still computes in 16-bit, so the math is unchanged. Speeding up prefill needs low-precision compute (W8A8, FP8).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
question: You split a program into `main.c` and `util.c`. `main.c` calls `parse()` defined in `util.c`. Which stage is the first one that needs to see both files?
options: The preprocessor, because it must find parse()
The compiler, because it must check parse() exists
The assembler, because it encodes the call instruction
The linker, because it resolves the call to parse() across object files
explain: Each .c file is preprocessed, compiled and assembled on its own; a declaration of `parse` (usually from a header) is enough for the compiler. The call is left as an undefined symbol plus a relocation in main.o. The linker is the first stage that sees both object files and patches the real address in.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
question: Right after `call square` executes, which statement is true?
options: rsp increased by 8 and the program counter points at square
rsp is unchanged; the return address is kept in a special register
rsp decreased by 8, the stack top holds the address of the instruction after the call, and the program counter points at square
rsp decreased by 8 and the stack top holds the address of square
explain: The stack grows down, so a push subtracts 8 from rsp. call pushes the return address (the next instruction in the caller), not the target, then jumps by writing square's address into the program counter.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
question: Why does x86-64 use a 4-level tree instead of one flat table indexed by the 36-bit page number?
options: A flat table cannot be cached in the TLB
Flat tables cannot hold physical frame numbers
Hardware cannot index arrays larger than 512 entries
A flat table would need 2^36 entries x 8 bytes = 512 GiB per process, mostly describing unused memory
explain: 2^36 x 8 bytes = 512 GiB (a gibibyte is 2^30 bytes), for every process. A tree only allocates the lower-level tables for regions actually in use, so a small process needs a few pages of page tables. The cost is the longer walk, which the TLB hides.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
question: Why must the end-of-sequence token after the answer be included in the trained targets?
options: It carries the reward signal for RLHF
It is required by the softmax
Otherwise the model never learns when to stop and keeps generating
It prevents the prompt from being masked
explain: Stopping is a learned prediction like any other. If the end token is masked, the model never sees a gradient for ending its turn and tends to run on, for example by writing the next user turn itself.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: In a PPO minibatch, a token has advantage -0.5 and its ratio has fallen to 0.7, with epsilon 0.2. What does this token contribute to the gradient?
options: A push to lower its probability further, because its advantage is negative
A push to raise its probability back to 1
Nothing, because negative advantages are always clipped
Nothing: the clipped term -0.4 is the minimum and does not depend on the weights
explain: rho x A = -0.35 and clip(0.7, 0.8, 1.2) x A = -0.4. The min is the clipped -0.4, a constant, so no gradient flows: the token was already made 30 percent less likely, past the 20 percent PPO allows per batch. If its ratio had been 1.3 instead, the unclipped -0.65 would be the min and the gradient would push it back down.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
question: Why does the engine keep df in the in-memory dictionary even for a pure Boolean search engine?
options: Boolean retrieval multiplies scores by df
It lets the planner order terms by list length before reading any postings
The merge algorithm needs df to know when to stop
It is needed to decompress postings
explain: Knowing each list's length up front lets the query optimizer intersect the shortest lists first. The merge itself stops when either pointer runs off its list, so it never needs df.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
options: two three
two
one two three
two three other
explain: switch jumps to case 2, then falls through into case 3 because nothing stops it, and the break after three leaves the switch before default. Forgetting break is a classic bug; when fallthrough is intended, write a comment saying so.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: `char a[] = "cat", b[] = "cat";` Does `if (a == b)` take the branch?
options: Yes, the two strings hold the same characters
It does not compile
Only if the compiler merges identical strings
No: == compares the addresses of two different arrays; use strcmp(a, b) == 0
explain: Both arrays decay to pointers to their first elements, and two distinct arrays never share an address, so the comparison is false; clang even warns `array comparison always evaluates to false`. strcmp compares the characters and returns 0 when they match.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
question: What does `int *f(int);` declare, compared with `int (*f)(int);`?
options: Both declare a pointer to a function returning int
The first is a pointer to an int, the second a function
Both declare a function returning a pointer
The first declares a function returning int *; the second, a pointer to a function returning int
explain: Without parentheses, `()` binds to f first, so f is a function (taking int) that returns `int *`. With `(*f)`, f is first a pointer, and what it points to is a function taking int and returning int.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Rust for C programmers: cargo, let, structs, enums and match
question: You add a variant `Triangle { b: f64, h: f64 }` to `Shape` but do not touch `area`. What happens?
options: `area` returns 0.0 for a triangle, the default for an unmatched value
It compiles with a warning and panics when a triangle reaches the match
The match falls through to the next arm, as a C switch without break does
rustc rejects the program with E0004, because the match no longer covers every variant
explain: Matches are exhaustive and checked at compile time. Adding a variant makes every match on the type that lacks it (and lacks a `_` arm) a compile error, which points you at each place that needs a decision. There is no default value and no fall-through.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
question: `v` is a `Vec<String>` with three elements. Which line compiles on its own?
options: `let s = v[1];`
`for s in v {}` followed by `println!("{}", v.len());`
`let s: &String = &v[1];`
`let first = &v[0]; v.push(String::new()); println!("{first}");`
explain: Borrowing an element is fine. Option 1 is E0507 (cannot move out of an index). Option 2 is E0382, because the loop consumed `v`. Option 4 is E0502: `first` is still used after `push` needs `&mut v`.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
question: A tree where each child needs a pointer back to its parent, and nodes are created and removed while the program runs. Which choice fits best?
options: Plain `&Node` references stored in each child
`Rc` from parent to children and `Weak` from child to parent (with `RefCell` where nodes must change)
Clone the parent into each child
explain: Nodes have no single owner whose scope covers every use, which is what plain references need. Cloning would give each child a separate copy rather than the real parent. `Rc` counts owners; a `Weak` back-pointer does not count, so parent and child do not keep each other alive in a cycle that leaks. `RefCell` allows mutation, checked at run time. This is the Book's tree design.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
question: $A$ has shape $3 \times 5$. Which input can it multiply, and what comes out?
options: A vector with 5 components; out comes a vector with 3
A vector with 3 components; out comes a vector with 5
Any vector; out comes a 3 x 5 matrix
A vector with 15 components; out comes a scalar
explain: Each row has 5 entries and is dotted with $\mathbf{x}$, so $\mathbf{x}$ needs 5 components. There are 3 rows, so 3 output components. An $m \times n$ matrix maps $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Orthogonality, projections and least squares
question: After a least-squares fit, the residual is $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}$. Which statement must hold?
options: r is the zero vector
r points in the same direction as y
r is orthogonal to every column of X
r has the same length as y
explain: The best fit is the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space, so the leftover is perpendicular to that space: $X^\top\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$. It is zero only if $\mathbf{y}$ was already reachable, which a tall noisy system almost never is.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
question: A classifier gives the correct class probability 0.9 on one example and 0.1 on another. Roughly how do their cross-entropy losses compare?
options: The 0.1 example costs about 22 times more (2.303 vs 0.105)
They are equal, since both are 0.4 away from 0.5
The 0.1 example costs exactly 9 times more
The 0.9 example costs more because it is more confident
explain: Cross-entropy is $-\ln p$: $-\ln 0.9 = 0.105$ and $-\ln 0.1 = 2.303$, a ratio of about 22. The log makes the cost grow without bound as the probability of the right answer goes to 0, which is exactly the confident-wrong case.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
question: You can't change the degree-9 model. Which change most directly reduces its overfitting?
options: Train longer to reach exactly zero training loss
Collect more training data from the same distribution
Evaluate on the training set instead
Increase the learning rate
explain: More data constrains the same model: median test RMS fell from 0.643 at N = 10 to 0.340 at N = 100. Training longer only drives it further into the noise, and evaluating on training data hides the problem.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
question: You ran 5-fold cross-validation to choose lambda, picked the best value, and want to report expected performance. What should you report?
options: The mean cross-validation score of the chosen lambda
The best single fold's score
The training score of the final model
The score on a test set that was never used for choosing lambda
explain: The chosen lambda won partly by luck on those folds, so its cross-validation score is optimistic. The scikit-learn guide keeps a test set aside for exactly this final evaluation.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
question: Connect-the-dots approximation of $\sin x$ gave worst errors 0.21, 0.070 and 0.019 with 4, 8 and 16 equal pieces. Roughly how many pieces give a worst error near 0.005?
explain: Each doubling cut the error by about 3 to 4 times, and the ratio was heading toward 4. One more doubling, to 32 pieces, gives about 0.0048. 64 would overshoot to around 0.0012.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Multi-class outputs: softmax, logits and the p minus y gradient
question: A 10-class network gives the true class probability 0.98 and some wrong class probability 0.015. What are $\partial L/\partial z$ for those two logits?
options: 0 and 0, because the prediction is already right
explain: $\partial L/\partial z_j = p_j - \delta_{yj}$. True class: 0.98 - 1 = -0.02, a small push up. Wrong class: 0.015 - 0 = 0.015, a small push down. Confident correct predictions produce small gradients, but never exactly zero.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
question: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss has stopped falling and is slowly rising. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Train for many more epochs until validation loss falls again
Report test accuracy at every epoch and pick the best one
Increase the model size
Stop at the epoch with the lowest validation loss (early stopping) or add regularisation
explain: Rising validation loss with falling training loss is the signature of overfitting. Early stopping or weight decay from the ML fundamentals course address it. Picking the epoch by test accuracy leaks the test set into model selection.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
question: A database scans a 50-page table in a loop, over and over, and has 49 frames for it. Which replacement policy gives the best hit rate?
options: LRU, because it keeps recently used pages
FIFO, because the scan is in arrival order
Random, because LRU and FIFO always evict the page needed next and hit 0% of the time
All three give the same hit rate
explain: In a loop larger than the cache, the least recently used page is exactly the one the loop needs next, so LRU (and FIFO, which evicts in the same order here) misses on every access. Random sometimes keeps the right pages and gets a non-zero hit rate. OPT would do better still.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
question: Thread A starts thread B and then sets `cfg = load_config()`. Thread B begins by reading `cfg->port`. It crashes occasionally. What kind of bug is this, and what is the usual fix?
options: An atomicity violation; wrap the read of cfg->port in a lock
An order violation; make B wait on a condition variable until A sets a flag after loading cfg
A deadlock; acquire locks in a global order
A data race on port; declare cfg volatile
explain: B assumes A's assignment has already happened: the intended order is not enforced. A lock alone does not fix it, since B could still take the lock first and see NULL. B must wait for a state variable (set by A after loading) using a condition variable, as in OSTEP's Mozilla fix. volatile does not create ordering.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
question: In data journaling, why must the file system wait for TxB, I[v2], B[v2] and Db to finish before writing TxE, instead of issuing all five writes at once?
options: Because the disk can only accept one write at a time
Because TxE must be written to the final location, not the journal
Because the disk may reorder a large write; TxE could land before Db, and replay would then copy garbage as if it were committed
Because waiting makes the journal smaller
explain: Disks schedule writes internally. If all five are issued together, TxE might hit the disk while Db has not. After a crash the transaction looks committed, and recovery would checkpoint garbage. Writing TxE only after the rest completes, as an atomic 512-byte write, closes the window.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Joint and marginal distributions, and the chain rule of probability
question: A language model gives probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.1 to three successive tokens, each conditioned on the tokens before it. What is the total log-probability (natural log) of the three tokens?
options: About -4.61, the sum of the three logs, equal to ln 0.01
About -1.54, the average of the three logs
0.8, the sum of the three probabilities
About -2.30, the log of the smallest probability
explain: By the chain rule the joint probability is 0.2 x 0.5 x 0.1 = 0.01, and the log of a product is the sum of logs: -1.61 - 0.69 - 2.30 = -4.61. The average, -1.54 per token, is minus the cross-entropy per token used as a training loss.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood
question: A language model assigns probability 0.5 to every correct next token in a validation set. What is its average cross-entropy (natural log), and what does minimizing it on training data correspond to?
options: 0.5; minimizing the error rate
About 0.693; maximizing the likelihood of the training tokens
About 0.693; minimizing the variance of the predictions
1.0; maximizing accuracy
explain: Cross-entropy averages -log of the probability given to the correct token: -ln 0.5 = 0.693. Minimizing average negative log-likelihood over the training data is exactly maximum likelihood estimation of the model's parameters.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
question: A test has 30% power for the smallest effect you care about, and it comes out significant. What is the main risk in the reported lift?
options: It is probably too small, since low power biases estimates toward 0
There is none: a significant result is trustworthy whatever the power
It is likely exaggerated, since only lucky overestimates cross the threshold in a weak test
The false positive rate has risen to 70%
explain: With low power, the runs that reach significance are mostly the ones where noise inflated the estimate, so the significant estimate overstates the truth (the exaggeration ratio). Alpha, the false positive rate, does not depend on power.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
question: At one budget your sweep trained only models smaller than the optimum, so the losses fall steadily and never turn up. What happens if you fit a parabola in $\log N$ to them?
options: The vertex lands on the optimum, because a parabola extrapolates the valley exactly
The fit raises an error, so you will notice the problem
Nothing; Approach 2 does not depend on which sizes you train
The vertex is extrapolated off one wall of a valley that is not exactly parabolic, so it can be biased
explain: In our repeated studies, sizes from 1/64x to 1x of the optimum pulled Approach 2's median forecast down to 75B against a truth of 96B, with no error raised. Approach 3, which fits the full formula to all runs, was not biased. Bracket each valley on both sides.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
question: A team will serve its model to millions of users for a year and needs a fixed quality bar. What does inference-aware scaling recommend?
options: Train the Chinchilla-optimal model, since it reaches the bar with the least compute
Train a smaller model on more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal, paying extra training compute to cut serving cost
Train the largest model the budget allows on fewer tokens, since bigger models are more sample-efficient
Train any size; inference cost does not depend on model size
explain: Serving costs about 2N FLOPs per token, so with heavy usage a smaller model that reaches the same loss by training longer has lower lifetime cost. Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute only. Bigger-and-shorter is Kaplan's advice and makes serving more expensive.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests
question: B beats A on MAP, 0.43 versus 0.37, over 8 queries. B wins on 2 queries and loses on 6. Which conclusion is justified?
options: B is better: MAP is the standard measure
Not established yet: check per-query differences with a paired test and add queries
A is better because it wins more queries
They are identical because 8 queries is too few to compute MAP
explain: A mean driven by one or two queries is fragile, and with 8 queries neither a t-test (p = 0.44) nor a sign test (p = 0.29) supports a general claim. Counting wins alone is also not a valid conclusion. Use more queries (about 50 is a common minimum) and a paired test.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
question: A dense-only search works well on natural questions but users complain that searching an exact SKU (stock keeping unit, a product code) like `KX-4471-B` returns similar-looking but wrong products. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase the embedding dimension from 384 to 1024
Lower the softmax temperature at query time
Switch from cosine to dot product
Add BM25 in parallel and fuse the lists with RRF
explain: Rare exact identifiers are where lexical matching is strongest and dense vectors are weakest. Hybrid retrieval keeps the dense model's paraphrase handling and adds exact-term recall. Temperature is a training-time setting; more dimensions or another similarity function do not create exact-match behavior.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
question: Why can GPT-2's tokenizer encode an emoji it never saw during tokenizer training, without an unknown token?
options: It has a fallback table of every Unicode character
The regex deletes characters it does not recognise
It maps any unseen character to the nearest known one
The emoji is UTF-8 bytes, and all 256 byte values are base tokens, so it can always be written as bytes
explain: The base vocabulary is the 256 byte values. Any string, emoji included, is a sequence of UTF-8 bytes, so in the worst case each byte is its own token. Merges only make common byte sequences shorter.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece in depth
question: With the 10 WordPiece merges from the toy corpus (the vocabulary includes n, ne, new, newe, ##e, ##r and ##er), encode ner by WordPiece's longest match, and by replaying the merges in learned order like BPE.
options: Both give ne ##r
Longest match gives ne ##r; replaying the merges gives n ##er
Longest match gives n ##er; replaying the merges gives ne ##r
Both give [UNK], because ner never appeared in training
explain: Longest match: ner is not in the vocabulary, ne is, then ##r. Replay: start n ##e ##r; (##e, ##r) was merge 6 and (n, ##e) merge 8, so ##er forms first and takes the e, giving n ##er. Same vocabulary, different procedure, different split.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Optimizers: momentum, Adam and decoupled weight decay
question: Early in training you notice Adam without bias correction takes steps about 3x larger than lr on step 1. Why?
options: The squared-gradient average v starts near 0 much more strongly than m, so m / sqrt(v) is inflated
Momentum accumulates over the first steps
epsilon is too large
The learning rate warms up automatically
explain: On step 1, m = 0.1 g and v = 0.001 g squared, so m / sqrt(v) = 0.1 / 0.0316 = 3.16. Dividing by 1 - beta_1 and 1 - beta_2 restores the ratio to 1.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
question: You accumulate gradients over 8 micro-batches but forget to divide each loss by 8. What is the effect with SGD?
options: Each step uses 8 times the mean gradient, so the effective learning rate is 8 times higher
Nothing, since each micro-batch loss is already a mean
The gradient is 8 times smaller than intended
BatchNorm statistics become averages over all 8 micro-batches
explain: backward() adds into .grad, so 8 undivided micro-batch means sum to 8 times the mean gradient. SGD's step is lr times that, as if lr were 8x. Adam would mostly hide it, because its step ignores gradient scale.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
question: An index returns 10 results for a query; 7 of them are among the true 10 nearest neighbors. A colleague says recall@10 is 0.7, but because the 7 are ranked in a different order than the exact ones, the real recall is lower. Who is right?
options: The colleague: order mismatches reduce recall@10
Neither: recall needs the distances, not the ids
You: recall@10 counts overlap with the true top 10, so it is 0.7
The colleague: recall@10 is only defined for exact order
explain: Recall@k, as defined in the HNSW paper, is the number of true nearest neighbors found divided by k. It is a set overlap; ranking quality inside the top k is a separate metric.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: The software supply chain: a map with every attack point
question: A project's git repository is clean, but the source archive attached to its release contains an extra build script that is not in git. Which stage was attacked?
options: Artifact publication: what was published differs from the source
Usage: the software was misconfigured
Package selection: users picked the wrong package
Source: someone pushed bad commits
explain: The source is clean, so the attack sits between source and users: the published artifact does not match the repository. That is SLSA threat F, and exactly what xz-utils did in 2024 (lessons 16 and 17).

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Maintainer takeover: when the real publisher ships malware
question: axios 1.x was already set up for trusted publishing from GitHub Actions. Why could the attacker still publish 1.14.1 from a stolen account?
options: The package still accepted traditional token and manual publishes alongside the trusted publisher
The attacker compromised GitHub Actions itself
Trusted publishing only applies to scoped packages
npm does not check two-factor authentication
explain: Configuring a trusted publisher adds a path; it does not close the others unless the package is set to disallow tokens. The axios post-mortem names publishing from a personal account as an avoidable risk.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: GitHub Actions attacks: pwn requests, injection and moving tags
question: A workflow uses `on: pull_request_target` and checks out the PR's head commit, but passes no secrets to any step. Is it safe?
options: No, but only for private repositories
Yes, because no secrets are referenced
Yes, if the job only runs npm install
No: the job still has a repository token with write access that the PR's code can read, by default also saved in .git/config by checkout
explain: Security Lab answers this exact question: the read/write GITHUB_TOKEN is in memory, and actions/checkout persists it on disk unless persist-credentials is false. npm install alone runs the PR author's install scripts.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
question: What is a VEX document for?
options: Encrypting an SBOM
Replacing the lockfile
Signing artifacts
Stating whether a product is actually affected by a known vulnerability, so users can skip non-issues
explain: CISA describes VEX as a form of security advisory that indicates whether a product is affected. It pairs with SBOMs: the SBOM says the component is present; VEX says whether that matters.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
question: After the tj-actions compromise, a public repository finds the action ran during the window. Why is rotating secrets urgent even though no data went to an attacker's server?
options: It is not urgent; encoding protects them
Because GitHub automatically shares secrets with forks
Because the malicious code also deleted the repository
Because the secrets were printed, encoded, into workflow logs that anyone can read in a public repository
explain: The payload dumped runner memory into the job log, double base64-encoded, which is trivially reversible. Public repository logs are public, so every secret in that run must be considered exposed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: A lab plans each new model's pretraining mix with a fixed 10-trillion-token budget: every year it removes old human text to make room for the latest scrape, which is increasingly model-written. Which strategy from this lesson does that resemble most?
options: Accumulate, because the dataset is being refreshed
Replace, because older real data are discarded and model output takes their place
The fresh data loop, which MAD found safe in all cases
None, because a 10-trillion-token budget is too large for collapse
explain: Holding the budget fixed while swapping out human text for model output drifts toward the replace setting, where errors compound. Keeping the original real data and growing the corpus matches the accumulate results.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
question: A logger issues one `write` per 40-byte log line and handles 200,000 lines per second. Which change cuts syscall overhead the most?
options: Switch from write to pwrite
Accumulate lines in a 64 KiB buffer and write when it fills or on a short timer
Call fsync after every line so the kernel batches better
Open the log file with O_APPEND
explain: Overhead scales with the number of calls. Buffering 64 KiB packs about 1,638 lines per call, so 200,000 calls per second become about 122. pwrite (write at a given offset) and O_APPEND (every write lands at the end of the file) change semantics, not call count, and fsync, which forces data to disk, adds an even more expensive call per line. Keep a flush timer so a crash or a quiet period does not hold lines forever.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE and copy-on-write
question: A program writes 100 MB into a MAP_SHARED file mapping, then the machine loses power before the program calls msync or munmap. What can you say about the file?
options: None of the writes are in the file
All of the writes are in the file, because shared mappings write through
The file is restored from the page cache on reboot
Any subset of the dirty pages may have reached the file
explain: The kernel writes dirty pages back whenever it chooses, so some may have reached the disk and others not, in no order you control. msync with MS_SYNC is how you force a range to disk and wait. This lack of ordering is why mmap-based databases still need a write-ahead log or shadow paging (as LMDB uses) to stay consistent.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
question: A closed-loop benchmark with 50 connections reports p99 = 4 ms. During the run the server had a 2 second GC pause. Which is the most likely truth?
options: p99 is about 4 ms; the pause produced at most 50 slow samples and those are correctly counted
The true p99 for users arriving at a constant rate is likely far higher, because requests that should have been sent during the pause were never sent or measured
p99 is lower than 4 ms because the pause reduced load
Percentiles are unaffected by coordinated omission; only the mean is
explain: Each of the 50 connections recorded one long sample during the pause and then nothing until it resumed. A constant-rate workload would have issued many requests during those 2 seconds, each waiting out the pause. Those are missing, so the reported p99 is biased low. wrk2's README shows a 1.4 s pause turning p99 from 6.04 ms (uncorrected) into 1.27 s.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: How a mobile network fits together: radio, core and the HLR
question: Why must a visited network contact the subscriber's home network when a roaming phone attaches?
options: Because only the home HLR/HSS holds the subscriber's key and profile, which the visited network needs to authenticate and serve the phone
To ask the home network to switch on the phone's radio
To download the phone's operating system updates
